etymology: From great and exchange (a mutual giving and receiving); a settled term for the double imputation at the heart of the gospel.
biblical_def: The Great Exchange is the church’s name for the wondrous transaction at the heart of justification, summed up in the apostle’s words: “For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.” In this exchange two things pass at once. Our sin and guilt were laid upon Christ, who, though He knew no sin of His own, was made sin for us and bore in His body on the tree the curse and condemnation we deserved. And His perfect righteousness—the active obedience of His whole life and the passive obedience of His death—is reckoned, imputed, to us who deserve none, so that we stand before God clothed in a righteousness not our own. He took our place under wrath; we take His place under favor. He was treated as the sinner that we might be treated as the righteous. This is double imputation: our sin to Him, His righteousness to us, neither by infusion nor by our own works, but by the free grace of God laying hold of Christ by faith alone. The dictionary holds the Great Exchange as the very marrow of the gospel and the ground of all assurance: the believer’s sin is fully answered and his righteousness fully supplied, both in Christ, so that there is now no condemnation to them which are in Him.
webster_summary: The gospel transaction in which the believer’s sin is imputed to Christ, who bore its curse, and Christ’s perfect righteousness is imputed to the believer—double imputation received by faith alone.
webster_full: THE GREAT EXCHANGE, the double imputation at the heart of justification.
Founded on 2 Corinthians 5:21, “he hath made him to be sin for us.”
Our sin and guilt laid upon Christ, who bore the curse we deserved.
His perfect righteousness imputed to us who deserve none.
Received not by works nor infusion, but by the free grace of God through faith alone.
scriptures: For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.
Isa 53:6
All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned every one to his own way; and the LORD hath laid on him the iniquity of us all.
Php 3:9
And be found in him, not having mine own righteousness, which is of the law, but that which is through the faith of Christ, the righteousness which is of God by faith:
Who his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree, that we, being dead to sins, should live unto righteousness: by whose stripes ye were healed.
corruption_summary: The exchange is denied or hollowed out by schemes that reject imputed righteousness for infused or self-attained righteousness.
corruption_paragraphs: The reigning corruption denies the imputation that makes the exchange possible. The Roman scheme replaces imputed righteousness with infused righteousness—a grace worked within that the sinner must cooperate with and complete—so that justification rests partly on the believer’s own renewed life. Various modern revisions of Paul likewise empty the exchange, denying that Christ’s active obedience is reckoned to us and reducing justification to covenant membership or future vindication by works.

The dictionary holds the double imputation as Scripture states it. He who knew no sin was made sin; we who have no righteousness are made the righteousness of God in Him. The exchange is forensic and complete, received by faith alone apart from works, and it is the only secure ground of a guilty sinner’s peace. To dilute it—making our righteousness partly our own, or Christ’s sin-bearing a mere example—is to rob the soul of the one robe that fits it for the presence of a holy God.
roots_summary: The phrase names the mutual transfer of Scripture: our sin to Christ, His righteousness to us, by imputation.
roots_lines: Greek logizomai — to reckon, impute, credit to one’s account; the verb of imputation.
Greek hamartia — sin; “he made him to be sin for us.”
Greek dikaiosunē — righteousness; “the righteousness of God in him.”
Luther’s phrase, the “happy exchange,” admirabile commercium.
The exchange is double: our guilt imputed to Christ, His righteousness imputed to us.
usage: The Great Exchange is preached as the marrow of the gospel and the ground of assurance.
It is summarized from 2 Corinthians 5:21 as the clearest statement of double imputation.
It is set against schemes of infused or self-attained righteousness.

etymology: From cross (Latin crux, the instrument of Roman execution) and Christ; the term for the crucifixion and its saving meaning.
biblical_def: The cross of Christ is the center of the Christian faith—the place where the Lord Jesus, by His death, made a full satisfaction to the justice of God for the sins of His people. Upon the cross Christ bore the curse of the broken law, being made a curse for us, as it is written, “Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree.” There He offered Himself a sacrifice, a propitiation that turned away the wrath of God; there He paid the ransom price of His own blood; there He reconciled His people to God, making peace through the blood of His cross. The cross is the wisdom and power of God to them that are saved, though it is to the natural man a stumblingblock and foolishness. Paul determined to know nothing among the Corinthians but Jesus Christ and Him crucified, and gloried in nothing save the cross by which the world was crucified to him and he to the world. The cross is not a defeat overtaken by the resurrection but the very triumph of God, where the Son in obedience drank the cup of wrath to the dregs and cried, “It is finished.” The dictionary holds the cross as the heart of the gospel: a real, substitutionary, penal, and propitiatory sacrifice, the ground of forgiveness, reconciliation, and every spiritual blessing, and the believer’s only boast.
webster_summary: The crucifixion of Christ and its saving meaning—a substitutionary, penal, propitiatory sacrifice satisfying God’s justice, bearing the curse, and reconciling His people to God.
webster_full: CROSS OF CHRIST, the crucifixion and its saving significance.
The place where Christ made full satisfaction to God’s justice for His people’s sins.
There He was made a curse for us, bearing the penalty of the broken law.
A propitiation turning away wrath and a ransom paid in His own blood.
To the natural man foolishness, but to the saved the wisdom and power of God.
scriptures: For the preaching of the cross is to them that perish foolishness; but unto us which are saved it is the power of God.
Gal 6:14
But God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, by whom the world is crucified unto me, and I unto the world.
Gal 3:13
Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us: for it is written, Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree:
Col 1:20
And, having made peace through the blood of his cross, by him to reconcile all things unto himself; by him, I say, whether they be things in earth, or things in heaven.
corruption_summary: The cross is stripped of penal substitution and recast as mere example, victory, or divine solidarity, emptying it of its atoning power.
corruption_paragraphs: The reigning corruption is the denial of penal substitution—the doctrine that Christ bore the penalty of sin in the sinner’s stead, suffering the wrath of God we deserved. Modern theology has recast the cross as a mere moral example of love (the old moral-influence theory of Abelard revived), or as a cosmic victory only, or as God’s solidarity with human suffering. Some have gone further and slandered the substitutionary atonement as “cosmic child abuse,” an attack on the very heart of the gospel.

The dictionary names these as corruptions and holds the cross as Scripture sets it forth. Christ was made a curse for us; He was the propitiation for our sins; He bore our sins in His own body on the tree; the chastisement of our peace was upon Him. The example, the victory, and the revelation of love are all real, but they all rest upon the substitution: it is precisely because Christ bore our penalty that His death is the supreme example of love, the decisive victory over sin and Satan, and the reconciliation of God and man. Remove the penal substitution and the cross has no saving power left.
roots_summary: The cross, an instrument of shameful death, became by Christ’s sacrifice the means of atonement and the believer’s glory.
roots_lines: Greek stauros — cross, the Roman instrument of execution.
Latin crux — cross, whence the English word.
Greek hilasmos — propitiation; the cross as the turning away of wrath.
Greek katara — curse; Christ “made a curse for us.”
The cross was the place of shame, made by Christ the place of triumph and glory.
usage: The cross of Christ is preached as the center of the gospel and the believer’s only boast.
Paul’s resolve to know nothing but Christ crucified shapes the priority of preaching.
It is defended against modern denials of penal substitutionary atonement.

etymology: From exalt (Latin exaltare, to lift up high) and Christ; the doctrine of the stages by which the humbled Christ was raised to glory.
biblical_def: The exaltation of Christ is the doctrine of the stages by which the Lord Jesus, after His state of humiliation, was raised to glory and dominion. The Reformed catechisms reckon the exaltation in four steps: His resurrection from the dead on the third day, His ascension up into heaven, His sitting at the right hand of God the Father, and His coming again to judge the world at the last day. Having humbled Himself and become obedient unto death, even the death of the cross, He was for that obedience highly exalted, given a name above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow. The exaltation is the Father’s public vindication of the Son and His acceptance of the finished work of the cross: the One condemned by men is justified by God, raised, enthroned, and crowned. From His exalted session Christ reigns over all things for His church, pours out the Holy Spirit, intercedes for His people as their great High Priest, subdues His enemies, and gathers His elect. The exaltation is also the pattern and pledge of the believer’s hope, for the same Lord who was abased and then glorified will raise and glorify all who are united to Him. The dictionary holds the exaltation as the triumphant counterpart to the humiliation: the way down was the way up, and the crucified Servant is now the reigning Lord.
webster_summary: The doctrine of the four stages—resurrection, ascension, session at God’s right hand, and return in judgment—by which the humbled Christ was raised to glory and dominion.
webster_full: EXALTATION OF CHRIST, the raising of the humbled Christ to glory.
Reckoned in four stages: resurrection, ascension, session, and return in judgment.
The Father’s vindication of the Son and acceptance of the finished work of the cross.
For His obedience unto death, He was given a name above every name.
The pattern and pledge of the believer’s own resurrection and glory.
scriptures: Php 2:9
Wherefore God also hath highly exalted him, and given him a name which is above every name:
Act 2:33
Therefore being by the right hand of God exalted, and having received of the Father the promise of the Holy Ghost, he hath shed forth this, which ye now see and hear.
Act 5:31
Him hath God exalted with his right hand to be a Prince and a Saviour, for to give repentance to Israel, and forgiveness of sins.
Eph 1:20
Which he wrought in Christ, when he raised him from the dead, and set him at his own right hand in the heavenly places,
corruption_summary: The exaltation is reduced to a symbol of the cause’s survival, denying the bodily resurrection, ascension, and present reign of Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the bodily and historical reality of each stage of the exaltation. Christ rose bodily, ascended visibly, sits enthroned at the Father’s right hand, and will return in person to judge. Against the liberal reduction that treats the resurrection as the survival of Jesus’ influence or the disciples’ rekindled faith, the dictionary holds that the same body that hung on the cross was raised, exalted, and glorified.

Where a corruption presses, it is the eclipse of Christ’s present reign. Many treat the ascension as a mere disappearance and forget that Christ is now actively reigning, interceding, and ruling all things for His church. The exalted Christ is not absent but enthroned; He governs history, subdues His enemies, and will not rest until every knee bows. The believer’s comfort is that his Saviour is not merely a memory but a living, reigning Lord, and that the way of humiliation followed by exaltation is the road his own life and death will travel in Christ.
roots_summary: The doctrine traces the upward stages by which the abased Christ was lifted to the throne.
roots_lines: Greek huperupsoō — to exalt to the highest place; “God also hath highly exalted him.”
The four stages: resurrection, ascension, session, and return in glory.
Set in deliberate contrast to the stages of humiliation.
The “right hand of God” — the place of honor, power, and royal rule.
Philippians 2 binds the humiliation and exaltation in one great hymn to Christ.
usage: The exaltation of Christ is taught in four stages in the Reformed catechisms.
It is preached as the Father’s vindication of the Son’s finished work.
Christ’s present reign and intercession are stressed against treating the ascension as mere absence.

etymology: From baptism (Greek baptisma, a washing, immersion) and Christ; the baptism of the Lord Jesus by John in the Jordan.
biblical_def: The baptism of Christ is the baptism of the Lord Jesus by John in the river Jordan at the outset of His public ministry, recorded in all four Gospels and rich in doctrine. John’s was a baptism of repentance for the remission of sins, and he protested that he had need to be baptized of Jesus; but the Lord answered, “Suffer it to be so now: for thus it becometh us to fulfil all righteousness.” The sinless One submitted to baptism not because He had any sin to confess, but to fulfill all righteousness, to identify Himself with the people He came to save, and to consecrate Himself to His mediatorial work. At His baptism the whole Trinity was manifested: the Son standing in the water, the Spirit descending upon Him as a dove, and the Father’s voice from heaven declaring, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” Thus the baptism is at once a revelation of the triune God, the public anointing of the Messiah for His office by the Spirit, and the Father’s open approval of the Son. The dictionary receives the baptism of Christ as the inauguration of His ministry and a standing witness to the Trinity, while noting that His baptism, unique to His person and office, is not the pattern for the meaning of Christian baptism, which is the believer’s confession of union with Christ in His death, burial, and resurrection.
webster_summary: The baptism of the sinless Christ by John in Jordan, to fulfill all righteousness and consecrate His ministry; the occasion of the Trinity’s manifestation and the Father’s approval of the Son.
webster_full: BAPTISM OF CHRIST, the baptism of the Lord Jesus by John in the Jordan.
Submitted to not for sin but “to fulfil all righteousness.”
The public anointing of the Messiah for His ministry by the Spirit.
The occasion of the Trinity’s manifestation: Son, Spirit as a dove, and the Father’s voice.
The Father’s open approval: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.”
scriptures: Mat 3:15
And Jesus answering said unto him, Suffer it to be so now: for thus it becometh us to fulfil all righteousness. Then he suffered him.
Mat 3:16
And Jesus, when he was baptized, went up straightway out of the water: and, lo, the heavens were opened unto him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove, and lighting upon him:
Mat 3:17
And lo a voice from heaven, saying, This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.
Luk 3:22
And the Holy Ghost descended in a bodily shape like a dove upon him, and a voice came from heaven, which said, Thou art my beloved Son; in thee I am well pleased.
corruption_summary: The Trinitarian witness of the baptism is denied by anti-Trinitarians, and its sinless purpose distorted by those who make Christ a repentant sinner.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the plain Trinitarian revelation at the Jordan: the Son in the water, the Spirit descending as a dove, the Father speaking from heaven—three distinct Persons, one God, manifest in a single scene. Against every anti-Trinitarian scheme, whether the modalism that makes Father, Son, and Spirit mere masks of one Person, or the unitarianism that denies the Son’s deity, the baptism of Christ stands as a clear scriptural witness to the holy Trinity.

A second corruption misreads the purpose of the baptism, suggesting that Christ submitted because He needed cleansing, and so denying His sinlessness. The text forbids it: He came to “fulfil all righteousness,” identifying with sinners He came to save, not confessing sins of His own. He was holy, harmless, undefiled. The dictionary holds both truths—the Son’s spotless purity and His gracious identification with His people—and distinguishes His unique baptism from Christian baptism, which signifies the believer’s union with Christ crucified and risen.
roots_summary: The baptism marks the anointing of the Messiah and the manifestation of the triune God at the Jordan.
roots_lines: Greek baptizō — to baptize, immerse, wash; John’s baptism of repentance.
Greek dikaiosunē — righteousness; “to fulfil all righteousness.”
The dove — the visible sign of the Spirit’s descent and anointing.
The voice from heaven — the Father’s testimony to the beloved Son.
The scene reveals the three Persons of the Godhead distinctly and at once.
usage: The baptism of Christ is cited as a clear scriptural manifestation of the Trinity.
“To fulfil all righteousness” is preached on Christ’s identification with His people.
It is distinguished from Christian baptism, which signifies union with the crucified and risen Christ.

etymology: From preeminence (Latin praeeminentia, supremacy, the first place) and Christ; the doctrine that Christ holds the first place in all things.
biblical_def: The preeminence of Christ is the doctrine that the Lord Jesus holds the first place—the supremacy, the headship, the chief seat—in all things, in creation, in redemption, and in the church. Paul sets it forth in the great Christological hymn of Colossians: Christ is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature; by Him were all things created that are in heaven and that are in earth; He is before all things, and by Him all things consist; and He is the head of the body, the church, who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, “that in all things he might have the preeminence.” The word “firstborn” here means not first in time, as if Christ were a creature, but first in rank, the heir and Lord of all. He is supreme as the eternal Creator, supreme as the risen Redeemer, supreme as the Head of His church, and it pleased the Father that in Him all fulness should dwell. The preeminence of Christ is therefore the great corrective to every rival—to the angel-worship and false philosophy at Colosse, and to every modern attempt to set Christ among many teachers, paths, or saviours. The dictionary holds the preeminence as the heart of true worship and right priorities: Christ is to have the first place in the believer’s affections, in the church’s worship, and in the whole created order, for in all things He must have the preeminence.
webster_summary: The doctrine that Christ holds the first place—supremacy and headship—in creation, redemption, and the church, that in all things He might have the preeminence.
webster_full: PREEMINENCE OF CHRIST, the doctrine of Christ’s first place in all things.
Set forth in the Christological hymn of Colossians 1.
Christ the image of God, the firstborn (first in rank) of creation, by whom all things were made.
The head of the body, the church, the firstborn from the dead.
It pleased the Father that in Him all fulness should dwell.
scriptures: Col 1:18
And he is the head of the body, the church: who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead; that in all things he might have the preeminence.
Col 1:16

For by him were all things created, that are in heaven, and that are in earth, visible and invisible, whether they be thrones, or dominions, or principalities, or powers: all things were created by him, and for him:
Col 1:17
And he is before all things, and by him all things consist.
Heb 1:3

Who being the brightness of his glory, and the express image of his person, and upholding all things by the word of his power, when he had by himself purged our sins, sat down on the right hand of the Majesty on high;
corruption_summary: Christ’s supremacy is denied by religious pluralism, which sets Him among many teachers, paths, and saviours.
corruption_paragraphs: The reigning corruption is religious pluralism—the doctrine that Christ is one teacher, path, or saviour among many, all leading to the same God. This directly contradicts the preeminence Scripture assigns Him. If by Him all things were created and in Him all fulness dwells, He cannot be set on a shelf beside Buddha, Muhammad, or the spiritual sages of the age. The Lord Jesus is not first among equals but supreme without rival, the only name under heaven given among men whereby we must be saved.

A subtler corruption arises within the church, where Christ is honored in word but displaced in practice—crowded out by programs, personalities, politics, and self. The preeminence of Christ rebukes this too: He is to have the first place in the church’s worship and the believer’s heart, not a place among many. The dictionary holds the doctrine in its full force against both the pluralism that denies His supremacy among the religions and the worldliness that erodes His supremacy within the church. In all things He must have the preeminence.
roots_summary: The word names Christ’s first place and supremacy, the rank that belongs to Him alone as Creator, Redeemer, and Head.
roots_lines: Greek prōteuō — to hold the first place, to be preeminent; “that he might have the preeminence.”
Greek prōtotokos — firstborn, here first in rank and heirship, not first in time.
Greek plērōma — fulness; all the fulness of God dwells in Christ.
Christ is supreme in creation, in resurrection, and as head of the church.
The word stands against every rival claim to the first place.
usage: The preeminence of Christ is preached against religious pluralism and idolatry.
Colossians 1 is the central passage for Christ’s supremacy over creation and the church.
The doctrine is applied to give Christ the first place in worship and the believer’s heart.

etymology: From son (the relation of a son to a father) and Christ; the doctrine of Christ as the eternal Son of God.
biblical_def: The sonship of Christ is the doctrine that the Lord Jesus is the eternal, only-begotten Son of God, the second Person of the Trinity, of one substance with the Father. His sonship is not adoptive, as ours is, nor a title earned at His incarnation or resurrection, but eternal and essential: He is the Son from everlasting, begotten of the Father before all worlds, not made, not created, true God of true God. The eternal generation of the Son means that the Father eternally communicates the one divine essence to the Son, without division, change, or beginning—a generation beyond time and beyond our comprehension, confessed in the Nicene Creed against the Arian denial. As the Son He is the brightness of the Father’s glory and the express image of His person; He does what He sees the Father do; He and the Father are one. In the incarnation the eternal Son took to Himself a true human nature, so that the same Person who is the eternal Son became also the Son of Man and, in His humanity, the Son of David. The Father’s voice at the baptism and the transfiguration declared Him the beloved Son. The dictionary holds the eternal sonship of Christ as a foundation of the Trinity and the gospel: only because the Saviour is the true and eternal Son could He reveal the Father, satisfy divine justice, and bring many sons to glory through union with Himself.
webster_summary: The doctrine that Christ is the eternal, only-begotten Son of God, of one substance with the Father, begotten not made—His sonship essential and everlasting, not adoptive or earned.
webster_full: SONSHIP OF CHRIST, the doctrine of Christ as the eternal Son of God.
Not adoptive nor earned, but eternal, essential, and of one substance with the Father.
Eternally begotten of the Father before all worlds, begotten not made.
Confessed in the Nicene Creed against the Arian denial of His deity.
The brightness of the Father’s glory and the express image of His person.
scriptures: Joh 3:16
For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life.
Joh 1:14
And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth.
Heb 1:5
For unto which of the angels said he at any time, Thou art my Son, this day have I begotten thee? And again, I will be to him a Father, and he shall be to me a Son?
Joh 5:23
That all men should honour the Son, even as they honour the Father. He that honoureth not the Son honoureth not the Father which hath sent him.
corruption_summary: The eternal sonship is denied by Arianism and its modern heirs, who make the Son a creature or a merely human Jesus adopted to divine status.
corruption_paragraphs: The reigning corruption is the ancient Arian denial, revived in modern forms, that the Son is a creature—the highest of creatures, perhaps, but not true God, “there was when He was not.” The Jehovah’s Witnesses and other groups perpetuate this error, mistranslating Scripture to make the Word “a god” and denying the eternal deity of the Son. The Nicene Creed was framed precisely to confess against them that the Son is “begotten, not made, being of one substance with the Father.”

A second corruption is the liberal and adoptionist reduction that makes Jesus a merely human figure later exalted to the status of Son—sonship as a reward or a title, not an eternal reality. The dictionary rejects both. The Son is eternally begotten of the Father, of one essence with Him, honored even as the Father is honored; to deny the Son is to dishonor the Father who sent Him. The whole gospel hangs upon it: a created or merely human saviour could not bear the infinite weight of divine justice nor join us to God, but the eternal Son could and did.
roots_summary: The doctrine confesses Christ’s eternal, essential sonship—begotten of the Father, of one substance, not made.
roots_lines: Greek monogenēs — only-begotten, unique; the only Son of the Father.
Greek homoousios — of one substance; the Nicene word for the Son’s unity of essence with the Father.
“Eternal generation” — the Father’s timeless communication of the divine essence to the Son.
Distinguished from adoption: ours is by grace, His is by nature and eternity.
The incarnate Son is also Son of Man and, in His humanity, Son of David.
usage: The eternal sonship of Christ is a foundation of the doctrine of the Trinity.
It is confessed against Arian and modern unitarian denials of Christ’s deity.
It grounds the believer’s adoption: the eternal Son brings many sons to glory.

etymology: From king and Christ; the doctrine of Christ’s kingly office, one of His three mediatorial offices.
biblical_def: The kingship of Christ is the doctrine of His kingly office, one of the three offices—prophet, priest, and king—by which He executes His work as Mediator. As King, Christ reigns over all things by right of His deity and by the Father’s appointment of the Mediator: all power in heaven and earth is given unto Him, and He must reign till He hath put all enemies under His feet. His kingship is exercised in three spheres. He rules His church by His Word and Spirit, gathering, governing, and defending His people, the sole Head and Lawgiver of His church, so that the conscience is bound by His commands alone. He rules providentially over the whole created order and the nations, governing history for the good of His church and the glory of God. And He will rule openly and visibly at His return, when every knee shall bow and He shall judge the world in righteousness. His kingdom is not of this world in origin or weapons—it comes not by sword or political conquest but by the gospel and the Spirit—yet it lays claim to every sphere, for there is no neutral ground over which the King does not reign. The dictionary holds the kingship of Christ as the comfort of His people and the claim upon all men: the crucified Servant is the crowned King, His reign is now and not yet, and the certain end of history is the universal acknowledgment of His Lordship.
webster_summary: Christ’s kingly office, one of His three mediatorial offices; He reigns over His church by Word and Spirit, over providence and the nations, and will reign openly at His return.
webster_full: KINGSHIP OF CHRIST, His kingly office as Mediator.
One of the three offices—prophet, priest, and king—of His mediatorial work.
All power in heaven and earth given unto Him; He must reign till all enemies are subdued.
He rules His church by Word and Spirit as its sole Head and Lawgiver.
He rules providence and the nations, and will reign openly at His return.
scriptures: And Jesus came and spake unto them, saying, All power is given unto me in heaven and in earth.
For he must reign, till he hath put all enemies under his feet.
Jesus answered, My kingdom is not of this world: if my kingdom were of this world, then would my servants fight, that I should not be delivered to the Jews: but now is my kingdom not from hence.
And he hath on his vesture and on his thigh a name written, KING OF KINGS, AND LORD OF LORDS.
corruption_summary: Christ’s kingship is either reduced to inward sentiment or distorted into a political program won by worldly power.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the present, real, and comprehensive reign of Christ, exercised by His Word and Spirit and not by carnal weapons. His kingdom is not of this world in its origin and means—it does not advance by the sword or by seizing the levers of political power—yet it is no mere inward feeling; it lays claim to every sphere and will be openly vindicated at His return. The error on one side privatizes His reign into a sentiment in the heart.

The error on the other side would make His kingdom a worldly political program won by force, confusing the church’s spiritual weapons with the magistrate’s sword. The dictionary keeps the balance the Scripture sets: Christ reigns now over all things for His church, He governs the conscience by His Word alone, He overrules the nations in providence, and He will return to reign visibly. His Lordship is total but His weapons are the gospel and the Spirit; the King who refused the crowd’s crown and the tempter’s kingdoms now reigns, and shall reign, King of kings and Lord of lords.
roots_summary: The doctrine sets forth Christ’s threefold reign—over His church, over providence, and in His coming glory.
roots_lines: Greek basileus — king; basileia — kingdom, reign, rule.
The threefold office: prophet, priest, and king, the munus triplex.
Christ reigns by right of deity and by the Father’s appointment of the Mediator.
His church-rule is by Word and Spirit; His sole headship binds the conscience.
“King of kings and Lord of lords” names His supreme and final dominion.
usage: The kingship of Christ is taught as one of His three mediatorial offices.
His sole headship over the church is cited against binding the conscience by human laws.
“My kingdom is not of this world” guards against both privatizing and politicizing His reign.

etymology: From love (Old English lufu) and Christ; the redeeming love of the Lord Jesus for His people.
biblical_def: The love of Christ is the redeeming love of the Lord Jesus for His people, a love that surpasses knowledge and constrains the believer’s whole life. It is an eternal love, set on His own before the foundation of the world; a free love, owing nothing to any worth or loveliness in its objects, who were yet sinners and enemies when He died for them; a particular love, by which the Good Shepherd lays down His life for the sheep, and Christ loved the church and gave Himself for it; a sovereign and effectual love, which does not merely offer but secures the salvation of the beloved; and an unchanging love, from which neither death nor life nor any creature can separate those who are in Christ Jesus. The supreme proof and measure of this love is the cross: greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends, and Christ commended His love in that while we were yet sinners He died for us. The love of Christ is not bare sentiment but costly self-giving unto death, and it both saves and transforms—the love of Christ constraineth us, says Paul, so that those who are loved live no longer to themselves but to Him who died for them and rose again. The dictionary holds the love of Christ as the warm center of the gospel, an electing, redeeming, persevering love, the believer’s deepest security and strongest motive to holiness.
webster_summary: The redeeming love of Christ for His people—eternal, free, particular, effectual, and unchanging—proved supremely at the cross and constraining the believer’s whole life.
webster_full: LOVE OF CHRIST, the redeeming love of the Lord Jesus for His people.
An eternal love, set on His own before the foundation of the world.
A free love, owing nothing to worth in its objects, who were sinners and enemies.
A particular and effectual love: the Good Shepherd lays down His life for the sheep.
An unchanging love, from which no creature can separate the believer.
scriptures: Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends.
Rom 5:8
But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.
Eph 5:25
Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it;
Rom 8:39
Nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.
corruption_summary: Christ’s love is sentimentalized into a feeling that affirms all and saves none, severed from the cross and from holiness.
corruption_paragraphs: The reigning corruption is the sentimentalizing of Christ’s love into a tolerant affection that affirms everyone as they are, demands no repentance, and threatens no judgment. This empties the word of its biblical meaning. The love of Christ is costly, going all the way to the cross to bear the wrath His people deserved; it is holy, calling its objects out of sin into obedience; and it is particular and effectual, actually saving those on whom it is set, not a vague benevolence toward all that saves no one in particular.

A further corruption uses “the love of Christ” to overthrow His commands—as if love meant approving what He forbids. But Christ Himself said, “If ye love me, keep my commandments,” and His love for us never sets His holiness aside. The dictionary holds the love of Christ in its full biblical weight: an electing, redeeming, persevering love proved by the cross, which both secures the believer forever and constrains him to live no longer to himself but to the One who loved him and gave Himself for him.
roots_summary: The doctrine sets forth Christ’s self-giving love—eternal in its source, the cross in its measure, holiness in its fruit.
roots_lines: Greek agapē — self-giving, sacrificial love; the love that goes to the cross.
Greek sunechō — to constrain, compel; “the love of Christ constraineth us.”
The cross is the supreme proof and measure of this love.
It is particular: Christ “loved the church, and gave himself for it.”
It is unchanging: nothing can separate the believer from it.
usage: The love of Christ is preached as eternal, particular, and effectual, proved at the cross.
“The love of Christ constraineth us” is cited as the great motive to holy living.
It is defended against sentimental misuse that severs love from holiness and judgment.

etymology: From Latin intercedere, to go between, to plead on another’s behalf; the priestly pleading of Christ for His people.
biblical_def: The intercession of Christ is the heavenly continuation of His priestly work, by which the exalted Lord, on the ground of His finished sacrifice, ever lives to plead for His people at the right hand of God. Having offered Himself once for sin, Christ did not lay down His priesthood but carried His one perfect sacrifice into the holy place not made with hands, there to appear in the presence of God for us. His intercession is not a renewed suffering nor a fresh offering, but the presentation of His accomplished work and the continual application of its benefits: He pleads His own blood, secures the pardon and acceptance of His people, obtains for them grace and help in time of need, answers the accusations of Satan, and ensures that their faith does not fail. Because He ever liveth to make intercession, He is able to save to the uttermost all that come unto God by Him. His intercession is effectual, never refused, coextensive with His atonement—He intercedes for those for whom He died—and it guarantees the perseverance and final salvation of every one of His own. He is also our Advocate with the Father; if any man sin, we have an Advocate, Jesus Christ the righteous. The dictionary holds the intercession of Christ as a chief comfort of the believer: his Saviour not only died for him once but lives for him now, pleading a finished work that cannot fail, so that no charge can stand against God’s elect.
webster_summary: Christ’s heavenly priestly pleading for His people on the ground of His finished sacrifice; effectual, never refused, securing their pardon, perseverance, and final salvation.
webster_full: INTERCESSION OF CHRIST, His heavenly priestly pleading for His people.
The continuation of His priesthood on the ground of His finished sacrifice.
Not a renewed offering, but the presentation of His accomplished work for us.
Effectual and never refused, coextensive with His atonement.
Because He ever liveth to intercede, He saves to the uttermost.
scriptures: Heb 7:25
Wherefore he is able also to save them to the uttermost that come unto God by him, seeing he ever liveth to make intercession for them.
Rom 8:34
Who is he that condemneth? It is Christ that died, yea rather, that is risen again, who is even at the right hand of God, who also maketh intercession for us.
My little children, these things write I unto you, that ye sin not. And if any man sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous:
Heb 9:24
For Christ is not entered into the holy places made with hands, which are the figures of the true; but into heaven itself, now to appear in the presence of God for us:
corruption_summary: Christ’s sole intercession is rivaled by the invocation of saints and Mary, and obscured where His present priestly work is forgotten.
corruption_paragraphs: The reigning corruption is the Roman invocation of saints and of Mary as intercessors and mediators alongside Christ. Scripture knows one Mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, and one Advocate with the Father; to seek the intercession of departed saints is to multiply mediators where God has appointed but one, and to dishonor the all-sufficient priesthood of the Son. The dictionary names this plainly: there is no intercessor in heaven for sinners but Jesus Christ the righteous.

A second corruption is practical rather than doctrinal—the forgetting of Christ’s present priestly work altogether, as though His ministry ended at the cross. But the same Christ who died now lives to intercede; His advocacy answers every accusation, His pleading secures every needed grace, and His unfailing intercession is the ground of the believer’s perseverance. Because He prays for His own that their faith fail not, none for whom He intercedes can finally be lost. To know that Christ ever lives to plead is the trembling believer’s strongest consolation.
roots_summary: The doctrine sets forth Christ’s continual heavenly pleading, the priestly “going between” on behalf of His people.
roots_lines: Latin intercedere — to go between, to plead on another’s behalf.
Greek entunchanō — to intercede, to plead with; “he ever liveth to make intercession.”
Greek paraklētos — advocate, one called alongside to plead; Christ our Advocate.
The intercession rests on and applies the finished sacrifice; it is no new offering.
It is coextensive with the atonement—He pleads for those for whom He died.
usage: The intercession of Christ is preached as the ground of the believer’s perseverance.
“He ever liveth to make intercession” assures that those Christ prays for cannot be lost.
Christ’s sole advocacy is cited against the invocation of saints and Mary.

etymology: From peace (Hebrew shālōm, Greek eirēnē) and God; the reconciled standing of the justified believer before God.
biblical_def: Peace with God is the reconciled standing of the justified believer before God—the end of enmity, the cessation of war, the restored favor that follows justification by faith. By nature fallen men are at enmity with God, children of wrath, alienated and enemies in their minds by wicked works; and God, being holy, is justly displeased with sinners. The gospel announces that this enmity is ended for those who are in Christ: “Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ.” This peace is not first a feeling but a relation—an objective reconciliation, a settled standing of favor, secured by the blood of the cross, where Christ made peace and reconciled us to God by His death. It is to be distinguished from the peace of God, the inward tranquility that guards the believer’s heart, though the one flows from the other. Peace with God is full and not partial, for justification is complete; it is permanent and not precarious, for the reconciliation rests on Christ’s finished work, not the believer’s performance; and it issues in access, joy, and hope. The dictionary holds peace with God as a chief blessing of justification: the war is over, the enmity slain at the cross, and the believer who was an enemy is now a reconciled child, at peace with the God against whom he had sinned, through the Lord Jesus Christ.
webster_summary: The reconciled standing of the justified believer before God—the end of enmity and restored favor, secured by Christ’s blood and received by faith; a settled relation, not first a feeling.
webster_full: PEACE WITH GOD, the reconciled standing of the justified believer.
The end of the enmity that fallen man bears toward God and God’s just displeasure with sinners.
“Being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ.”
An objective reconciliation secured by the blood of the cross, not first a feeling.
Distinguished from the peace of God, the inward tranquility that flows from it.
scriptures: Rom 5:1
Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ:
Col 1:20
And, having made peace through the blood of his cross, by him to reconcile all things unto himself; by him, I say, whether they be things in earth, or things in heaven.
Eph 2:14
For he is our peace, who hath made both one, and hath broken down the middle wall of partition between us;
Rom 5:10
For if, when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son, much more, being reconciled, we shall be saved by his life.
corruption_summary: Peace with God is cheapened into a feeling of well-being apart from the cross, or presumed without justification by faith.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that peace with God is first a relation, not a feeling, and that it is purchased by blood and received by faith. The modern reduction of peace to a vague inner serenity, attainable by anyone through meditation, therapy, or positive thinking, severs it from the cross where alone the enmity was slain. There is no peace with God apart from the reconciliation Christ made by His death and apart from justifying faith that lays hold of Him.

A second and deadly corruption is the false peace of the unconverted—the presumption of those who are at ease in Zion, who say “Peace, peace” when there is no peace, because they have never been justified by faith nor reconciled to God. The prophets and the apostles alike warn against this counterfeit. The dictionary holds the true and the false apart: real peace with God follows real justification, rests on Christ’s finished work, and is the secure portion of the believer; the counterfeit is the dangerous calm of a soul still at war with God and unaware of it.
roots_summary: The phrase names the reconciled relation of the believer to God—enmity ended, favor restored, by the blood of the cross.
roots_lines: Hebrew shālōm — peace, wholeness, well-being, the restored relation with God.
Greek eirēnē — peace; “we have peace with God.”
Greek katallassō — to reconcile, to change from enmity to friendship.
Peace with God (a relation) is distinguished from the peace of God (an inward tranquility).
The peace is made “through the blood of his cross.”
usage: Peace with God is preached as a chief blessing of justification by faith.
It is distinguished from the inward peace of God that flows from it.
The false peace of the unconverted is warned against from the prophets’ “peace, peace.”
